category: Core vocabulary: camping and the outdoors

entries.meaning: An area set aside for people to camp, usually with numbered sites and restrooms. ---
examples: The campground fills up fast on holiday weekends.
There are two campgrounds on the north side of the lake.
We pulled into the campground just before dark.

entries.meaning: A numbered spot at a campground where you may pitch a tent. ---
examples: We reserved a tent site near the water.
The walk-in tent sites are quieter.
Our tent site had a flat patch of gravel.

entries.meaning: A padded bag you zip yourself into to sleep outdoors. ---
examples: My sleeping bag is rated for twenty degrees.
We hung the sleeping bags out to dry.
He crawled into his sleeping bag without taking his socks off.

entries.meaning: Someone who walks long distances in the countryside for pleasure. ---
examples: A hiker passed us going the other way.
The trail was full of hikers by ten in the morning.
An experienced hiker always checks the forecast.

entries.meaning: The activity of hiking into the wilderness carrying everything you need on your back. ---
examples: We got into backpacking the summer after college.
Backpacking teaches you how little you actually need.
She bought a lighter stove for backpacking.
entries.русский: пеший поход с рюкзаком и ночёвками

entries.meaning: The place where a trail starts, usually with a parking lot and a sign. ---
examples: We left the car at the trailhead.
Both trailheads were closed for repairs.
There's a map posted at the trailhead.

entries.meaning: A marked path through country or forest made for walking. ---
examples: This hiking trail runs eight miles along the ridge.
The park has hiking trails for every ability.
The hiking trail was muddy after all that rain.

entries.meaning: A light rod that holds up the fabric of a tent. ---
examples: One tent pole snapped in the wind.
The tent poles fold up into a short bundle.
Thread the tent pole through the sleeve first.

entries.meaning: A short spike driven into the ground to hold a tent down. ---
examples: I hammered the last tent stake in with a rock.
We lost two tent stakes in the tall grass.
The ground was too hard for a tent stake.

entries.meaning: The waterproof sheet that goes over a tent to keep the rain off. ---
examples: Put the rainfly on before you go to bed.
Cheap rainflies leak at the seams.
Water was pooling on top of the rainfly.

entries.meaning: A cord running from a tent to the ground to steady it in wind. ---
examples: Tighten that guy line on the windward side.
I tripped over one of the guy lines in the dark.
A loose guy line lets the tent flap all night.
entries.contrast: Guy is said GY, like the word for a man, but here it means a steadying rope.

entries.meaning: Thin strong nylon cord used for a hundred jobs around camp. ---
examples: I keep fifty feet of paracord in my pack.
We hung the food bag with paracord.
A little paracord fixed the broken strap.

entries.meaning: A large sheet of waterproof material used as cover or shelter. ---
examples: We strung a tarp over the picnic table.
Two tarps kept the firewood dry.
Spread the tarp under the tent.

entries.meaning: A thin mat that insulates you from the ground while you sleep. ---
examples: My sleeping pad went flat around midnight.
Foam sleeping pads never puncture.
Roll the sleeping pad out under your bag.

entries.meaning: Bedding rolled into a bundle for carrying and sleeping outdoors. ---
examples: He tied his bedroll to the back of the saddle.
Our bedrolls were still damp in the morning.
She unrolled her bedroll next to the fire.

entries.meaning: An inflatable mattress you blow up to sleep on. ---
examples: The air mattress went soft around three in the morning.
We packed two air mattresses for the tent.
Pump up the air mattress before it gets dark.

entries.meaning: A portable light in a case that you can carry or hang up. ---
examples: Hang the lantern from the tent pole.
Both lanterns run on the same batteries.
The lantern threw shadows all over the campsite.

entries.meaning: A small light on an elastic band worn on your forehead. ---
examples: A headlamp leaves both your hands free.
We hiked the last mile by headlamp.
Pack spare batteries for your headlamp.
entries.contrast: For a car, Americans say headlight; a headlamp is the one you wear.

entries.meaning: A device that makes stream or lake water safe to drink. ---
examples: Run it through the water filter first.
Backpacking water filters have gotten a lot lighter.
The water filter clogged up with silt.

entries.meaning: Water that is safe to drink. ---
examples: There's no potable water past this point.
The sign said the spigot was potable water.
Carry enough potable water for two days.
entries.contrast: Said POH-tuh-buhl, not POT-uh-buhl.

entries.meaning: A small portable burner for cooking outdoors. ---
examples: The camp stove boils a liter in three minutes.
Both camp stoves use the same fuel.
Set the camp stove on level ground.

entries.meaning: A nesting set of pots, plates and utensils for camp cooking. ---
examples: Everything in the mess kit packs into the pot.
The kids each got their own mess kits.
Wash the mess kit away from the stream.

entries.meaning: A camping utensil that is a spoon at one end and a fork at the other. ---
examples: I ate the whole dinner with a plastic spork.
We lost two sporks on that trip.
A titanium spork weighs almost nothing.

entries.meaning: A folding hand tool with pliers, blades and other small tools built in. ---
examples: He fixed the stove with his multitool.
Good multitools are heavy but worth it.
There's a bottle opener on the multitool.

entries.meaning: A small knife with blades that fold into the handle. ---
examples: He whittled a stick with his pocketknife.
Both pocketknives need sharpening.
I always carry a pocketknife on the trail.
entries.contrast: The k in knife is silent, and the plural is irregular: pocketknives.

entries.meaning: A small axe you can swing with one hand. ---
examples: Split the kindling with the hatchet.
We keep two hatchets in the camp box.
Keep the hatchet in its sheath when it's not in use.

entries.meaning: A tool with a heavy blade on a long handle for chopping wood. ---
examples: The axe was stuck in a stump behind the cabin.
Both axes could use sharpening.
He swung the axe and split the log clean through.
entries.contrast: Americans often spell it ax. The plural axes is said AK-siz here, but AK-seez when it means more than one axis.

entries.meaning: A climber's tool with a pick and a shaft, used on snow and ice. ---
examples: She stopped her slide with the ice axe.
Two ice axes were strapped to his pack.
You need an ice axe above the snowline.
entries.contrast: Often spelled ice ax in American English.

entries.meaning: An adjustable walking pole that takes weight off your knees on a trail. ---
examples: One trekking pole is better than none.
My trekking poles collapse down to fit in the pack.
Shorten your trekking pole on the way up.

entries.meaning: A small backpack big enough for one day's water, food and jacket. ---
examples: A twenty-liter daypack is plenty.
Leave the big packs and take daypacks up to the summit.
My daypack weighs almost nothing empty.

entries.meaning: A waterproof bag that rolls shut to keep gear dry. ---
examples: Put the camera in a dry bag.
We lashed two dry bags to the raft.
Everything in the dry bag stayed perfectly dry.

entries.meaning: A small bag with a drawstring for packing gear into a backpack. ---
examples: My sleeping bag lives in a red stuff sack.
Color-coded stuff sacks keep things easy to find.
Everything went into one stuff sack.

entries.meaning: A small box or pouch of bandages and medicine for treating injuries. ---
examples: There's a first aid kit in the trunk.
Both first aid kits were missing tape.
Restock the first aid kit before every trip.

entries.meaning: A thin shiny sheet that reflects body heat, carried for emergencies. ---
examples: A space blanket weighs two ounces and folds up tiny.
They wrapped him in two space blankets.
There's a space blanket in the bottom of my pack.

entries.meaning: A liquid or spray put on skin or clothes to keep insects away. ---
examples: Put on some insect repellent before dusk.
The insect repellent wore off after an hour.
We ran out of insect repellent on the second night.

entries.meaning: A strong pepper spray carried for defense against bears. ---
examples: Keep the bear spray on your hip, not in your pack.
Rangers sell bear spray at the visitor center.
He never hikes here without bear spray.

entries.meaning: A metal locker at a campsite where food is stored away from bears. ---
examples: Everything with a smell goes in the bear box.
Each site has its own bear box.
He forgot to latch the bear box overnight.

entries.meaning: A fine mesh screen hung up to keep biting insects out. ---
examples: The mosquito net over the door had a hole in it.
We slept under mosquito nets on the porch.
Zip the mosquito net shut behind you.
entries.contrast: In mosquito the qu sounds like sk: muh-SKEE-toh.

entries.meaning: Waterproof clothing worn to stay dry outdoors. ---
examples: Pack your rain gear even if the sky looks clear.
My rain gear is still hanging in the garage.
Everyone dug out rain gear when the clouds came over the ridge.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: never rain gears. Count it as pieces of rain gear.

entries.meaning: A stick used for balance and support while walking. ---
examples: He cut himself a walking stick from a fallen branch.
The old walking sticks by the door are for guests.
A walking stick helps a lot on the way down.
entries.contrast: A walking stick is also the name of a thin insect that looks like a twig.

entries.meaning: A ring or hollow in the ground where a campfire is built. ---
examples: Every site has a fire pit and a picnic table.
The old fire pits were full of ash and cans.
Keep the fire inside the fire pit.

entries.meaning: Very dry material that catches a spark and starts a fire. ---
examples: Dry grass makes good tinder.
We couldn't find any tinder after three days of rain.
He shredded some bark for tinder.
entries.contrast: Sounds close to tender, but tinder is what you light a fire with.

entries.meaning: A small block, stick or tool used to get a fire going. ---
examples: A wax fire starter burns even when it's wet.
He keeps a few fire starters in his pack.
Light the fire starter and stack the kindling over it.

entries.meaning: A hard gray stone that makes sparks when struck with steel. ---
examples: He struck the flint until a spark caught.
The riverbed was full of flints.
You can start a fire with flint and a knife blade.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A small device that makes a flame for lighting a fire or stove. ---
examples: Does anybody have a lighter?
We brought two lighters and a box of matches.
The lighter wouldn't work in the wind.

entries.meaning: A small piece of glowing coal or wood left from a fire. ---
examples: An ember popped out and burned a hole in his sleeve.
We cooked the potatoes right in the embers.
Pour water on every ember before you leave.

entries.meaning: A stack of cut wood kept for burning. ---
examples: There's a woodpile behind the cabin.
Snow covered both woodpiles.
Grab a couple of logs off the woodpile.

entries.meaning: A soft white candy that people toast over a campfire. ---
examples: His marshmallow caught fire and fell in the coals.
The kids ate a whole bag of marshmallows.
Hold the marshmallow over the embers, not the flame.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say MARSH-mel-oh, not MARSH-mal-oh.

entries.meaning: A campfire treat of toasted marshmallow and chocolate between two crackers. ---
examples: She ate one s'more and asked for another.
We make s'mores every night at camp.
You can't have a campfire without a s'more.
entries.русский: сморы (десерт из зефира, шоколада и крекеров)
entries.contrast: Written with an apostrophe: it is short for some more.

entries.meaning: A snack mixture of nuts, dried fruit and sometimes candy, carried on hikes. ---
examples: We split a bag of trail mix at the overlook.
There's trail mix in the side pocket.
He picks all the chocolate out of the trail mix.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: some trail mix or a bag of trail mix, never trail mixes.

entries.meaning: A wooden table with attached benches, set up outdoors. ---
examples: We ate dinner at the picnic table.
All the picnic tables were taken by noon.
Somebody carved their initials into the picnic table.

entries.meaning: A light folding chair you take to a campsite. ---
examples: He fell asleep in a camp chair by the fire.
The camp chairs fold into little bags.
Pull up a camp chair and sit down.

entries.meaning: An overnight stay outdoors, often for a group of kids. ---
examples: The troop has a campout every spring.
Rain washed out both campouts last year.
It was his first campout without his parents.
entries.contrast: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: we camped out.

entries.meaning: A trip on which you sleep outdoors in a tent or camper. ---
examples: We're planning a camping trip for Labor Day.
Their camping trips always end up in the same spot.
The camping trip got rained out.

entries.meaning: The main camp a party works out of on a long climb or expedition. ---
examples: We rested two days at base camp.
Both base camps sat below the glacier.
They radioed base camp every evening at six.

entries.meaning: A hike you finish and come back from in a single day. ---
examples: It's an easy day hike to the falls.
The guidebook lists twenty day hikes near the city.
We only had time for a short day hike.

entries.meaning: A short trip away from home for pleasure. ---
examples: The whole family came on the outing.
Weekend outings to the lake are a tradition here.
Bad weather cut the outing short.

entries.meaning: Long-distance walking over rough country, often for several days. ---
examples: Three weeks of trekking left him ten pounds lighter.
Trekking at that altitude is slow going.
She bought new boots for the trekking season.

entries.meaning: Someone walking an entire long trail end to end in one season. ---
examples: A thru-hiker came through camp looking for a resupply.
Thru-hikers start in Georgia in early spring.
The thru-hiker had been walking for four months.
entries.contrast: Thru is a deliberate short spelling of through, used only in this hiking term.

entries.meaning: A simple shelter with a sloping roof and one open side. ---
examples: We slept in a lean-to to stay out of the rain.
There are three lean-tos along this stretch of trail.
He built a lean-to out of branches and a tarp.
entries.contrast: Keep the hyphen, and the plural is lean-tos.

entries.meaning: A rough overnight camp made without a tent. ---
examples: They spent the night in a bivouac under an overhang.
Cold bivouacs are part of alpine climbing.
The storm turned our summit day into an unplanned bivouac.
entries.contrast: The ou is just an uh sound: BIV-uh-wak.

entries.meaning: A round tent on a wooden frame, rented at some campgrounds. ---
examples: We booked a yurt instead of a tent site.
The park's yurts have beds and a small heater.
The yurt stayed warm all night.

entries.meaning: A narrow bed, often one of two stacked in a cabin or shelter. ---
examples: I got the top bunk by the window.
The cabin sleeps eight in four bunks.
He was asleep in his bunk before nine.

entries.meaning: An official who looks after a park or forest and the people in it. ---
examples: A ranger checked our permit at the trailhead.
The rangers close the road when it ices over.
Ask the ranger where the bears have been active.

entries.meaning: An official paper allowing you to hike or camp in a protected area. ---
examples: You need a wilderness permit to sleep back there.
Wilderness permits go fast in July.
We picked up our wilderness permit at the ranger station.
entries.русский: разрешение на поход в заповедную зону
entries.contrast: The noun permit stresses the first syllable, PUR-mit; the verb per-MIT stresses the second.

entries.meaning: A large protected area of land kept by the government for public use. ---
examples: We spent a week in the national park.
The western national parks get crowded in July.
You need a pass to enter the national park.

entries.meaning: A protected park run by a state rather than the federal government. ---
examples: There's a nice state park twenty minutes from here.
Most state parks charge a small day-use fee.
The state park has cabins you can rent by the night.

entries.meaning: An area of land protected so that its plants and animals are left alone. ---
examples: The nature preserve is open from dawn to dusk.
Dogs aren't allowed in most nature preserves.
A boardwalk runs through the nature preserve.

entries.meaning: A building at a park where you get maps, permits and information. ---
examples: Stop at the visitor center for a trail map.
Both visitor centers close at five.
There's a small museum in the visitor center.
entries.contrast: Americans write center; the British write centre.

entries.meaning: A short marked path with signs explaining the plants and animals along it. ---
examples: The nature trail is a half mile loop.
Schools bring kids out to the nature trails every spring.
Numbered posts along the nature trail match the pamphlet.

entries.meaning: Remote wild land far from roads and towns. ---
examples: You need a permit to camp in the backcountry.
Cell service disappears once you're in the backcountry.
They spent five days in the backcountry without seeing anyone.

entries.meaning: Thinly settled forest country far from any town. ---
examples: He grew up in the backwoods of Maine.
There's a cabin out in the backwoods with no power.
The road into the backwoods washes out every spring.
entries.contrast: Always ends in -s; there is no singular a backwood.

entries.meaning: The open air and the natural world outside buildings. ---
examples: He loves the great outdoors.
The outdoors is where those kids are happiest.
Two weeks in the outdoors did her a world of good.
entries.contrast: Always ends in -s but takes a singular verb: the outdoors is.

entries.meaning: Protected land where roads, vehicles and building are not allowed. ---
examples: No bikes are allowed in the wilderness area.
Several wilderness areas border the park.
The trail crosses into the wilderness area at the pass.

entries.meaning: A sharp turn in a trail that zigzags up a steep slope. ---
examples: There's a bench at the last switchback.
We counted forty switchbacks on the way up.
Don't cut the corner on a switchback — it wrecks the trail.

entries.meaning: Making your way through thick brush where there is no trail. ---
examples: The last mile was pure bushwhacking.
Bushwhacking in shorts is a bad idea.
We saved time with a little bushwhacking along the ridge.
entries.русский: движение без тропы, продирание через заросли

entries.meaning: A pile of stones built to mark a trail or a summit. ---
examples: Follow the cairn across the bare rock.
Somebody knocked over half the cairns up there.
The cairn is the only marker above the treeline.
entries.contrast: The ai sounds like air: KAIRN, one syllable.

entries.meaning: A sign, blaze or symbol showing the way along a trail. ---
examples: We missed a trail marker and walked an extra mile.
The trail markers are blue rectangles on the trees.
There's a trail marker at every junction.

entries.meaning: A place where two or more trails meet. ---
examples: Turn left at the trail junction.
The trail junctions are all signed up here.
We waited for the others at the trail junction.

entries.meaning: A point on a route saved or marked so you can navigate to it. ---
examples: Save the car as a waypoint before you start.
He loaded a dozen waypoints onto his watch.
The spring is the last waypoint before the summit.

entries.meaning: The skill of finding your way using a map, compass or landmarks. ---
examples: Navigation gets hard once the fog rolls in.
The course covers basic wilderness navigation.
He's better at navigation than anyone in the group.

entries.meaning: A map that shows hills and valleys with contour lines. ---
examples: Bring a topographic map and know how to read it.
The store sells topographic maps of the whole range.
The topographic map showed a much steeper climb than I expected.

entries.meaning: The sport of finding checkpoints across country with a map and compass. ---
examples: She got into orienteering through her scout troop.
Orienteering teaches you to trust the compass over your instincts.
There's an orienteering meet in the state forest on Saturday.

entries.meaning: A narrow bridge for people on foot. ---
examples: Cross the creek on the footbridge.
High water took out both footbridges.
The footbridge sways a little when you walk on it.

entries.meaning: A place where you get across a river, or the act of doing it. ---
examples: The river crossing is dangerous after a storm.
There are four river crossings on this route.
We waited until morning to make the river crossing.

entries.meaning: A shallow place where you can walk or drive across a stream. ---
examples: The ford is just below the bend.
Both fords were knee-deep in June.
We took our boots off at the ford.

entries.meaning: A raised stone you step on to cross shallow water or mud. ---
examples: One stepping stone was slick with moss.
We hopped across on the stepping stones.
She missed the last stepping stone and soaked one boot.

entries.meaning: The land along the edge of a river. ---
examples: We camped on the riverbank above the rapids.
Willows grow along both riverbanks.
The riverbank was steep and slippery.

entries.meaning: A small circle of water turning back against the main current. ---
examples: Pull into that eddy behind the boulder.
The eddies below the falls are full of foam.
His paddle got caught in an eddy.
entries.contrast: Plural eddies: the y becomes ies. It sounds like the name Eddie.

entries.meaning: A deep spot in a creek or river where people swim. ---
examples: There's a swimming hole a mile down the trail.
Every kid in town knows the best swimming holes.
We jumped off the rock into the swimming hole.

entries.meaning: The sport of riding a river in an inflatable boat. ---
examples: We went rafting on the Colorado.
Rafting season runs from May to September.
The rafting was tamer than the brochure suggested.

entries.meaning: Fast rough river water broken into foam over rocks. ---
examples: That stretch of whitewater scared me.
The river drops into whitewater below the bridge.
He's been paddling whitewater since he was twelve.

entries.meaning: The activity of traveling in a small narrow boat with a double paddle. ---
examples: Kayaking on the lake is calm and easy.
She took up sea kayaking last year.
We did some kayaking before breakfast.

entries.meaning: The activity of traveling in an open boat moved with a single paddle. ---
examples: Canoeing is easier with two people.
The upper lake is perfect for canoeing.
The camp teaches canoeing to the younger kids.

entries.meaning: A stretch of land where you carry a boat between two bodies of water. ---
examples: The portage around the falls is a half mile.
There are five portages on this route.
We carried the canoe over the portage in two trips.

entries.meaning: A padded vest that keeps you afloat in water. ---
examples: Nobody gets in the boat without a life vest.
There are four life vests under the seat.
Buckle the life vest across your chest.
entries.contrast: Life vest is the usual American term; the British say life jacket.

entries.meaning: A metal loop with a spring gate used to connect ropes and gear. ---
examples: Clip the rope into the carabiner.
He had a dozen carabiners on his harness.
Make sure the carabiner is locked.
entries.contrast: Stress the third syllable: kair-uh-BEE-nur.

entries.meaning: The rope hold that protects a climber from a fall. ---
examples: She set up a belay at the top of the pitch.
The guide checks every belay before anyone climbs.
He shouted that the belay was ready.

entries.meaning: Someone who climbs rock, ice or mountains. ---
examples: A climber fell on that route last summer.
Two climbers were already on the wall at sunrise.
The climber rested on a narrow ledge.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: KLY-mur.

entries.meaning: The sport of climbing up steep rock faces with ropes and gear. ---
examples: Rock climbing got me over my fear of heights.
He teaches rock climbing on weekends.
There's good rock climbing an hour north of town.

entries.meaning: Climbing short hard routes on low rocks without ropes. ---
examples: An afternoon of bouldering leaves your fingers raw.
Bouldering is hard on your fingers.
The gym has a bouldering wall in the back.

entries.meaning: The sport of climbing high mountains, often over snow and ice. ---
examples: Mountaineering takes years of experience.
He wrote a book about mountaineering in Alaska.
The club runs a mountaineering course every winter.

entries.meaning: Going down a rock face by sliding in a controlled way along a rope. ---
examples: We practiced rappelling off a low cliff.
Rappelling is faster than climbing back down.
The guide checked our knots before the rappelling started.
entries.contrast: Americans say rappelling; the British say abseiling.

entries.meaning: A climb up a mountain or slope. ---
examples: The ascent took us six hours.
He has made three ascents of that peak.
The last part of the ascent is on loose rock.
entries.contrast: Sounds almost exactly like assent, which means agreement.

entries.meaning: A climb or walk down from a high place. ---
examples: The descent is harder on the knees than the climb.
Both descents follow the same gully.
We started the descent as the weather turned.
entries.contrast: Said just like dissent, which means disagreement.

entries.meaning: A place on rock where you can put your foot while climbing. ---
examples: She found a foothold just above the crack.
The footholds get tiny near the top.
There was no foothold on that smooth slab.

entries.meaning: A place on rock that you can grip with your hand while climbing. ---
examples: The only handhold was a thin flake of rock.
The wet handholds made it dangerous.
He felt around for a handhold above his head.

entries.meaning: A narrow flat shelf of rock sticking out from a cliff. ---
examples: We ate lunch on a ledge above the valley.
Birds nest on the ledges of that cliff.
The ledge was just wide enough to stand on.

entries.meaning: A steep rough mass of rock sticking out of a hillside. ---
examples: A hawk was circling the crag.
Climbers come from all over for these crags.
We ate lunch in the shade of the crag.

entries.meaning: A narrow crack in rock or a wall. ---
examples: A small plant was growing out of a crevice.
Lizards hide in the crevices during the heat of the day.
He wedged his fingers into the crevice.
entries.contrast: A crevice is a small crack in rock; a crevasse (kruh-VAS) is a deep split in a glacier.

entries.meaning: A deep open crack in a glacier or ice field. ---
examples: A snow bridge hid the crevasse completely.
The glacier is full of crevasses by late summer.
They roped up before crossing the crevasse field.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, unlike crevice (KREV-is), which means a small crack in rock.

entries.meaning: The final hard effort to reach the top of a mountain. ---
examples: The summit push starts at two in the morning.
Bad weather turned back two summit pushes that week.
They rested a full day before the summit push.

entries.meaning: The long top edge of a ridge, seen against the sky. ---
examples: The trail follows the ridgeline for three miles.
You can see two ridgelines from the porch.
Wind hits you hard once you're on the ridgeline.

entries.meaning: The height on a mountain above which trees do not grow. ---
examples: We camped just below the treeline.
The treelines here sit around eleven thousand feet.
There's no shelter above the treeline.

entries.meaning: The height on a mountain above which snow lies all year. ---
examples: The snowline is much lower in May.
Their route stays below the snowline.
We camped a thousand feet under the snowline.

entries.meaning: A low hill at the base of a mountain range. ---
examples: They live out in the foothills.
The road climbs through the foothills for an hour.
Every foothill around here is covered in oak.
entries.contrast: Almost always used in the plural: the foothills of the Rockies.

entries.meaning: The sloping side of a mountain. ---
examples: A fire had burned the whole mountainside.
The mountainsides were still green in September.
Their cabin sits halfway up the mountainside.

entries.meaning: A narrow channel cut into a slope by running water. ---
examples: The trail drops into a steep gully.
Spring runoff carved new gullies in the hillside.
We scrambled up the gully to reach the ridge.
entries.contrast: Plural gullies: the y changes to ies.

entries.meaning: A part of a rock face that sticks out over the ground below. ---
examples: We waited out the storm under an overhang.
The route goes over two small overhangs.
Water dripped off the edge of the overhang.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable, OH-vur-hang; the verb stresses the last.

entries.meaning: Rock that sticks up out of the ground through the soil. ---
examples: There's a granite outcrop with a view at the top.
Hawks sit on those outcrops all afternoon.
We took a break on a sunny outcrop.

entries.meaning: A wide stretch of large loose rocks you have to climb across. ---
examples: The boulder field slowed us down for an hour.
Two boulder fields lie between here and the lake.
Watch your ankles in the boulder field.

entries.meaning: Loose broken stone lying on a steep mountain slope. ---
examples: The last half mile is all scree.
Coming down the scree is faster than going up.
Loose scree slid out from under my boots.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: a slope of scree, never screes.

entries.meaning: A wide area of snow that stays on a mountain through the summer. ---
examples: We crossed the snowfield early, while it was still firm.
The snowfields shrink a little every year.
Bring an ice axe for that snowfield.

entries.meaning: A dense group of bushes or small trees growing close together. ---
examples: A deer crashed off into the thicket.
Thickets of willow line the creek.
We lost the trail in a thicket of brush.

entries.meaning: An open grassy space inside a forest. ---
examples: The trail opens into a sunny glade.
Deer feed in these glades at dusk.
We pitched the tent at the edge of the glade.

entries.meaning: The low bushes and plants growing under the trees in a forest. ---
examples: The underbrush here is too thick to walk through.
Something moved in the underbrush behind the tent.
Crews cleared the underbrush to slow down fires.
entries.contrast: American; the British usually say undergrowth.

entries.meaning: One of the thin sharp green leaves of a pine tree. ---
examples: A pine needle was stuck to the bottom of my sock.
The ground was soft with pine needles.
Pine needles smell wonderful when you crush them.

entries.meaning: A high place with a wide view, or the tower built there. ---
examples: The lookout is a mile up the fire road.
Old fire lookouts are scattered along the range.
We watched the sunset from the lookout.
entries.contrast: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: look out.

entries.meaning: A tall wooden or steel tower where someone watches for forest fires. ---
examples: The trail ends at an old fire tower.
Most of these fire towers are no longer staffed.
You can see three states from the fire tower.

entries.meaning: A wide view of the landscape, especially from a high place. ---
examples: The trail opens up to a vista of the whole valley.
There are pullouts with vistas every few miles.
That vista is worth the climb.

entries.meaning: A pullout beside a road where you stop to look at the view. ---
examples: Pull in at the next scenic overlook.
There are scenic overlooks all along the parkway.
We ate our sandwiches at a scenic overlook.

entries.meaning: Looking at the stars for pleasure. ---
examples: The desert is perfect for stargazing.
A clear, moonless night is best for stargazing.
Stargazing is better away from town lights.

entries.meaning: Searching in the wild for food such as berries, nuts or mushrooms. ---
examples: He teaches a class on foraging in the spring.
Foraging for mushrooms takes real knowledge.
We did a little foraging along the creek.

entries.meaning: Camping with comfortable beds and hotel-like extras. ---
examples: This isn't camping, it's glamping.
They booked a glamping site with a real mattress.
Glamping got popular around here a few years ago.

entries.meaning: A dangerous drop in body temperature from being cold and wet. ---
examples: Wet cotton in cold wind can cause hypothermia.
He was showing early signs of hypothermia.
Hypothermia kills more hikers than falls do.

entries.meaning: The harmful condition of not having enough water in your body. ---
examples: Dehydration sneaks up on you at altitude.
The headache was probably dehydration.
Drink before you're thirsty to avoid dehydration.

entries.meaning: Weakness, dizziness and sweating caused by too much heat. ---
examples: Two hikers were treated for heat exhaustion.
Heat exhaustion can turn serious fast.
Get into the shade at the first sign of heat exhaustion.
entries.contrast: The h in exhaustion is silent: ig-ZAWS-chuhn.

entries.meaning: Illness caused by spending too long in strong sunshine. ---
examples: Wear a hat or you'll get sunstroke.
He came down with sunstroke on the second day.
Sunstroke left her dizzy for hours.

entries.meaning: Headache and nausea caused by thin air high in the mountains. ---
examples: Altitude sickness hit her at twelve thousand feet.
Going up slowly helps prevent altitude sickness.
He had altitude sickness the whole first night.

entries.meaning: A common American plant whose oil gives people an itchy rash. ---
examples: That whole bank is covered in poison ivy.
He got poison ivy on both arms.
Leaves of three — that's poison ivy.

entries.meaning: A tiny sharp piece of wood stuck in your skin. ---
examples: I got a splinter carrying firewood.
She pulled two splinters out with tweezers.
The splinter was too deep to reach.

entries.meaning: The small itchy swelling left where a mosquito has bitten you. ---
examples: I woke up with a mosquito bite on my eyelid.
His ankles were covered in mosquito bites.
Try not to scratch that mosquito bite.

entries.meaning: The act of staying alive in dangerous conditions. ---
examples: The class covers survival in cold weather.
Shelter matters more than food for short-term survival.
He wrote a book about survival in the backcountry.

entries.meaning: A group of people organized to look for someone who is lost. ---
examples: A search party went out at first light.
Two search parties combed the north side of the ridge.
The search party found her cold but unhurt.

entries.meaning: A bright burning light fired or lit to signal for help. ---
examples: He set off a flare from the ridge.
There are two flares in the emergency kit.
A flare is visible for miles at night.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like flair, which means a natural talent.

entries.meaning: A large fire burning through trees and brush. ---
examples: Smoke from the forest fire reached us two states away.
Dry summers mean more forest fires.
The forest fire closed every trail in the canyon.

entries.meaning: An official rule against lighting fires because of dry conditions. ---
examples: There's a fire ban in effect until it rains.
Fire bans start earlier every summer.
The fire ban means no campfires, only stoves.

entries.meaning: The mark a foot or shoe leaves in soft ground. ---
examples: There was one footprint in the mud by the creek.
We followed his footprints through the snow.
The rain washed every footprint off the trail.

entries.meaning: The mark left in soft ground by an animal's foot.
examples: That paw print is bigger than my hand.
There were paw prints all around the cooler.
She photographed a paw print next to her boot for scale.
